column4: The source-section’s warning example is an enemy advance that should make hearers take precautions; here the fighters take حذرهم and weapons because the enemy may attack while they pray.
The section says the fire can be angry; here Hell nearly bursts from الغيظ and its keepers ask whether a نذير came, joining the raging fire and warning in one scene.
The section’s alarm is meant to produce precaution, but these inmates say a نذير came and they كذبنا; the next ayah supplies the raging fire that receives them.
The source-section root ش ق و names both wretchedness and hardship; this earlier context sets فُجورها against تقواها before the chapter names its most wretched person.
The section opposes الأشقى to الأتقى; this same surah says the one who تزكى succeeds, giving the counter-side to its named wretch.
The source section makes the most wretched the one led to hardship; here the one who دسّاها fails, opposite the soul that purified itself in 91:9.
The source section explicitly links its الأشقى to 91:12; the verse names the one who rises among Thamud as أَشْقَاهَا, putting the label in a concrete story.
This is the command that precedes the people’s denial in 91:14: the Messenger names God’s she-camel and her drink, completing what the wretch and his people reject.
The section’s warned person كَذَّبَ and turned away; here the people كَذَّبُوهُ and hamstrung the she-camel after the Messenger’s command.
The section contrasts the one protected from fire with the wretch; here the reminder benefits من يخشى, the one who fears, identifying who can receive the alarm.

The source-section root ج ن ب describes moving someone away from harm; here the same form yetجنبها says the most wretched avoids the reminder, the reverse of the pious person being kept from fire in 92:17.
The section’s root ص ل ي explains entering and enduring fire; this verse says the reminder-avoider يَصْلَى النار الكبرى.
This completes 87:12’s fire scene: its entrant neither dies nor lives there, specifying the cost of the wretch’s avoidance of reminder.
The section pairs the spared أَتْقَى with giving and self-purification; this adjoining contrast says the one who تزكى succeeds.
The source section names لظى as the fire’s name and glosses its root as pure flame; this verse identifies the fire as لظى.
The section explains ص ل ي through enduring fire and roasting; لظى here is described as stripping the flesh of the scalp, a specific bodily effect of the flame.
The section says the fire calls the one who turned away; this verse repeats أدبر وتولى as the person Leza calls, directly connecting rejection to the flame.
The source section quotes this exact continuation: Leza calls the one who جمع فأوعى, joining the fire with the gatherer who hoards.
The source-section gloss for تلظى includes burning in anger; here the fire sees its inmates from afar and is heard in تَغَيُّظٍ and roaring.
The source section distinguishes entering from remaining in fire; here its inmates are thrown into a narrow place in chains, turning the source’s protective barrier into confinement.
This completes the narrow-fire scene of 25:13: the inmates call for one destruction, then many, giving the anguish behind the section’s warning.
The source-section root ش ق و names wretchedness opposite happiness; this judgment divides people into شَقِيّ and سعيد before specifying their ends.
This identifies the wretched party from 11:105 as being in the fire, where they sigh and sob; it joins the section’s ashqa label directly to its flame.
The source-section root ص ل ي includes remaining in the fire; this verse says the wretched abide there with sighing and sobbing, subject to God’s will.
The happy party’s lasting Garden answers the section’s contrast between the wretch who enters and the most mindful person kept away.
The section warns of a fire; here Hell is made visible to whoever sees, a direct scene of the threatened fate being shown.
The section’s ashqa enters the fire; this passage begins its matching account with the one who transgressed.
The section’s wretch turns away from the warning; here the transgressor is defined by preferring الحياة الدنيا.
This names Hell as the transgressor’s abode, the reverse of the section’s person who is kept away from fire.
This gives the opposite disposition to the wretch: one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains the soul from desire.
The one who fears has the Garden as abode; this is the positive destination corresponding to the section’s al-atqa being removed from the fire.
The section says an alarm is not effective if its hearer turns away; here warning or no warning makes no difference to those who will not believe.
This defines the receptive counterpart to the section’s fire-denier: only one who follows the reminder and fears the Merciful is warned in a beneficial sense.
The same warning boundary appears here: disbelievers do not believe whether the Prophet warns them or not, unlike the section’s protected, fearful recipient.
After 2:6’s rejected warning, hearts and hearing are sealed; it gives a concrete blockage opposite the section’s alarm that should reach and move its hearers.
Those in the punishment admit a warner did come before being told to taste it; this directly stages the section’s warning refused before fire.
Lot warned his people of God’s assault, but they disputed the warnings; this is the section’s unheeded alarm in a specific prophetic scene.
The Prophet is told to say he is only a نذير before severe punishment, matching the section’s single first-person alarm before the blazing fire.
The verse says “We warned you” of near punishment and makes the threatened day concrete; it echoes the section’s warning of an approaching fire and reckoning.
This uses the source-section root ص ل ي directly: the condemned face enters نارًا حامية, a hot fire.
The command to remind matches the section’s alarm; it establishes that the messenger’s role is to recall, leaving the hearer’s response consequential.
The messenger is not a controller over them; that specifies the limit of the section’s warning voice, whose alarm cannot itself make the hearer take precaution.
The person who turns away and disbelieves is the section’s 92:16 figure, specified here as one who leaves the reminder.
This gives the consequence of turning away in 88:23: God subjects that person to the greatest punishment, completing the warning sequence.
The command to remind with the Quran is directed to one who fears God’s warning, matching the section’s contrast between the fearful recipient and the wretch.
Noah is told to warn his people before painful punishment comes, a direct formulation of the section’s alarm before the fire.
Noah identifies himself as a clear warner, matching the section’s single voice that delivers the signal.
The warning’s requested response is to worship, fear God, and obey; the section says alarm is completed when hearers take precaution.
The warning is followed by promised forgiveness and a deferred appointed term, showing what responding to the alarm may avert.
Noah asks whether his people wonder that a reminder came through one of them to warn them, so they may fear and receive mercy; the alarm has a protective aim.
They denied Noah, so he and the believers were saved while the deniers drowned; it gives a concrete division between response to warning and its rejection.
The person who turns away from the reminder and wants only worldly life matches the section’s denier who turned away before facing the fire.
The source-section root ش ق و includes distress and hardship; here the Quran is explicitly not sent to make the Prophet تَشْقَى, a different use of that root.
The Quran is a reminder for one who fears; this clarifies the recipient side of the section’s alarm and the atqa kept from fire.
Turning away from remembrance leads to a constricted life; the source section likewise pairs turning away with the route made hard and the fire reached by the wretch.
This is the turned-away person’s question after being raised blind, continuing the consequence of 20:124’s refusal of remembrance.
The answer says God’s signs came and were forgotten; this names the neglected warning behind the person’s post-resurrection state.
This concludes the refusal sequence by saying the Hereafter’s punishment is more severe and lasting, fitting the section’s warning of the final fire.
The source-section root ص ل ي describes entering fire; this verse threatens to cast the denier into Saqar.
Saqar neither spares nor leaves anything, specifying the severity of the fire the section warns about.
The section glosses تلظى as pure flame and ص ل ي as enduring heat; here the fire scorches human skin.
The question asks what brought the speakers into Saqar, framing the specific failures that follow as causes of entering fire.
The inmates say they did not feed the poor; this reverses the giver whom the whole surah 92 sets against its miser, in the section’s fire-bound division.
They say they denied the Day of Judgment, directly matching the section’s person who denied and turned away before being warned of fire.
The source-section root ص ل ي is used here for entering a blazing fire, سعيرًا, after judgment.

The verse says everyone will come to the Fire, while 19:72 immediately saves those who feared God; its relation to the section’s “only the wretch enters” depends on how وُرُودها is understood, since arrival or passage is also read.
The next verse says God saves those who feared Him and leaves wrongdoers there; this is a direct instance of the section’s atqa kept away from fire.
Being moved far from the Fire and admitted to the Garden is called success, a direct outcome for the section’s protected person.
The people who give food to the poor, orphan, and captive set up the righteous action that precedes protection from the Day’s evil in 76:11, as in the section’s giving and taqwa.
They say they feed only for God’s face and seek neither reward nor thanks, matching the section’s giving for God rather than repayment.
Their reason for feeding is fear of a grim day; this links the section’s protective taqwa to the fear that moves one to give.
The source section explicitly cites this root و ق ي: God protects them from the evil of that day after their God-directed giving.
The muttaqin are placed in gardens and bliss, the other side of the section’s wretch who enters fire.
This says their Lord protected them from the punishment of Hell, a direct example of the section’s shield for the God-fearing.
The angels ask God to protect believers from the punishment of Hell; this prayer states the section’s shield image as a plea for protection.
The same prayer asks that believers enter gardens, completing the escape from fire with the opposite destination.
The prayer asks God to protect them from evil deeds; this matches the source-section root و ق ي as making a barrier against what is feared.
Those promised good are kept far away from Hell, an exact parallel to the section’s يُجَنَّبُها for the most mindful.
The saved do not even hear Hell’s hiss, completing the distance from its flame in 21:101.
The greatest terror does not grieve them; this adds the safety from fear that the section’s protection from fire implies.
The believer in Pharaoh’s court says he calls his people to salvation while they call him to the Fire, making the section’s warning choice explicit.
God protects the believer from Pharaoh’s plotting, a concrete use of the source section’s protection idea before the contrasting punishment.
Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening and then enter harsher punishment, opposite the person God protects in 40:45.
God delivers those who fear Him and evil does not touch them; this states the section’s protective result in the same fearful group.
Hell’s keepers ask whether warners came, and the disbelievers admit the warning; this joins the section’s alarm to the fire it announces.
The deniers are told to enter Hell and remain there, the outcome opposite the section’s pious person kept from it.
Those who feared their Lord are led to the Garden instead, completing the section’s contrast between ashqa and atqa.
The Garden’s residents praise God for fulfilling His promise; this completes the rescue side of the fire/Garden contrast begun in 39:73.
The command اتقوا النار directly joins the source-section’s root و ق ي, protective fear, to the very fire that 92:14 warns about.
This repeats the command to guard against the prepared Fire, a direct Quranic formulation of the section’s protective barrier.
The command قوا أنفسكم asks people to protect themselves and their families from Fire, directly matching the section’s self-placement within a shield.
Believers ask God to protect them from the punishment of Fire, showing divine shielding as the answer to the section’s warning.
The prayer قنا عذاب النار asks to be kept safe from Fire, a concise response to the section’s alarm.
The servants pray for God to turn the punishment of Hell away from them; the source-section root ج ن ب describes being moved away from harm.
They call Hell an evil place to settle, completing their plea to be kept away from it in 25:65.
The Quran says clothing protects from heat and violence; the source-section root و ق ي explains taqwa as placing a protective layer against what is feared.
David is taught armor that protects people from battle; this gives a physical protective counterpart to the source-section’s dictionary image of a shield at one’s side.
The verse says whoever is protected from his own شح succeeds; the section opposes the miser with the one who gives and is spared the Fire.
Those who اجتنبوا false gods and turn to God receive good news; this is active avoidance in the source-section root ج ن ب, paired here with a positive outcome.
The command فاجتنبوه tells people to avoid harmful practices and promises success; it is the active avoiding sense of the source-section root ج ن ب.
The wrongdoers are enclosed by a سرادق of fire; this reverses the source-section’s protective barrier, since here a boundary traps rather than shields from the flame.
A wall with a door divides believers inside mercy from hypocrites outside with punishment; it makes the section’s separating shield a visible boundary between different ends.
They take oaths as جُنَّة, a shield, then turn from God’s path and face punishment; unlike the section’s true taqwa barrier, this shield is deceptive and does not protect.
The same false shield of oaths is used while they deny and block God’s path; it contrasts the section’s protective taqwa with a cover that leads toward punishment.
The condemned are told to go to a three-branched shade, a supposed shelter inside the fire scene that the next verse exposes as no refuge.
The shade neither cools nor protects from flame; it is the direct reversal of the source-section’s siper, a shelter that fails against the danger.
The same fire throws sparks like great palaces, giving the moving, vivid flame that the source glosses for تلظى.
The next verse compares the sparks with yellow camels, continuing the section’s image of flame as rapidly moving fire.
Hell is called a مرصاد for the transgressors, a waiting place for the person whose turn-away leads to fire in the section.
The transgressors remain in Hell for ages; this matches the source-section explanation that entering fire can mean remaining bound to it.
These people did not expect an account, a concrete form of the denial that precedes the section’s threatened Fire.
They rejected God’s signs, matching the section’s one who كذب and turned away before entering fire.
The inmates are told to taste punishment that only increases, specifying the severity behind the section’s warning.
The next passage gives the God-fearing success, the opposite group to the transgressors for whom Hell is a waiting place.
The God-fearing receive a reward from their Lord; this completes the protective destination introduced for them in 78:31.
The verse condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending it; this is the same gather-and-hoard figure whom Leza calls in the section’s cited 70:18.
The hoarded wealth is heated in Hell and brands foreheads, sides, and backs; the source-section root ج ن ب also names a shield by the side, here reversed into an exposed side scorched by fire.
The person who counts and hoards wealth matches the gatherer whom Leza calls in the section’s quoted 70:18.
He supposes his wealth will make him immortal, specifying the self-sufficiency that the section sets against fearing the warning.
The hoarder is thrown into the Crusher, directly joining the wealth image to a fire fate.
The Crusher is called نار الله الموقدة, connecting the section’s pure flame and fiery warning with a fire kindled by God.
The fire rises over hearts, specifying the reach of the section’s dangerous flame.
The fire is closed over the condemned, reversing the section’s protective enclosure around the God-fearing.
The closing fire is extended in columns, completing the confinement scene of 104:8.
Pursuit of greater accumulation distracts people, echoing the section’s gatherer who hoards before Leza calls him.
The accumulation continues until visiting the graves, carrying the section’s warning toward the afterlife.
The accumulators are told they will see Hell, a direct consequence after the section’s hoarder and fire warning.
They see it with certainty, intensifying the threatened fire from 102:6.
They will be questioned about نعيم, giving an accounting after the section’s reminder that wealth does not avail at the fall.

The source-section root ن و ر explains نار through flickering light; here a kindled fire first lights the surroundings and then its light is taken away. It is a different parable and a tentative lexical contrast with the section’s punitive flame.

The source section’s naked alarm is a visible sign at distance and names نار through the source root ن و ر; here Musa sees a far-off fire and goes toward it for news or a brand. The relation is tentative because this fire guides rather than threatens.
Musa tells his family he sees a fire and will bring news or a brand; this repeats the distant visible signal, but reverses the section’s warning fire into guidance.
Musa sees fire from the mountain’s side and goes to it for news or a burning brand; this is a repeated distant-fire signal, tentatively contrasted with the section’s dangerous flame.
The source-section root ص ل ي includes roasting meat; Abraham’s calf is described as حنيذ, a roasted meal, giving that secondary fire sense a hospitable rather than punitive scene.
This repeats Abraham’s حنيذ calf; it activates the source-section root ص ل ي’s cooking sense as a contrast to entering the blazing fire.
The source-section dictionary glosses عسر as bending or opposition and links it to the route made difficult; this verse pairs العسر with ease, a counterpoint to the section’s turn toward hardship.
The repeated promise that ease accompanies العسر preserves the section’s named hardship root while offering its opposite outcome.
This verse calls the Judgment Day عسيرًا for disbelievers; the source section glosses ash-shaqā as hardship and joins the wretch to the difficult end.

People report that an enemy force has gathered against the believers; the report increases their faith, and they rely on God. This closely matches the section’s alarm of an approaching enemy and the response of taking precautions.
The believers return with favor and no harm touches them, completing the response to the warning in 3:173 and echoing the section’s protection from danger.
The command to take precautions and advance in groups gives another concrete military form of the source section’s warning about an enemy advance and the precautions that should follow.
The command to prepare strength against an enemy is a specific parallel to the section’s example of learning of an assault and making oneself ready.
The Prophet is told that the Quran warns its hearers and whoever it reaches; this specifies how the section’s alarm travels from one voice to its audience.
The Prophet is sent as a warner, and the verse names the companions of Hell; it joins the warning role to the fire outcome in the section.
The Book warns of severe punishment while giving good news to believers, joining the section’s alarm and its division between the fire-bound and the protected.
The believers’ abiding reward completes the good-news side introduced alongside warning in 18:2, complementing the section’s fire and shelter contrast.
Thamud’s denial is stated immediately before the rise of their most wretched person in 91:12, completing the section’s link between the ashqa and rejected warning.
The passage says people prefer the nearer life after describing the reminder-avoiding wretch; this makes explicit the preference behind the section’s turning away from warning and its fire.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, completing 87:16’s contrast and clarifying why the section’s fire warning concerns a lasting end.
This verse says the disbelievers remain in the Fire without death or relief; the next verse recalls that a warner came, completing the section’s entry-and-warning sequence.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily; this sharpens the giver-versus-miser contrast that frames the section’s spared and fire-bound people.
The dwellers of the Garden are protected from the punishment of Hell; this is another direct use of the source-section root و ق ي for the pious kept away from fire.
The deniers are pushed toward Hell, a forceful entry scene for the fire that the section warns about.
They are told that this is the Fire they used to deny, matching the section’s sequence from warning to denial and punishment.
The inmates are asked whether the punishment is magic or whether they cannot see, continuing the exposure of the fire-deniers.
The command to burn in it uses the source-section root ص ل ي and directly describes enduring the flame.
The people of the left are given shade of black smoke; this apparent shelter is the opposite of the section’s protective shield, and the next verse states its failure.
That smoke-shade is neither cool nor beneficial, completing the failed-shelter image that reverses the section’s siper.
The passage identifies the condemned person as an astray denier, matching the section’s wretch who denied the warning before entering fire.
This denier’s reception is boiling water, the next stage of the punishment described before the burning in 56:94.
The verse names burning in Hell, using the source-section root ص ل ي and joining denial to fire.
Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly are said to eat fire and burn in the Blaze; this joins misuse of wealth to the source section’s wealth-hoarder and fire fate.
Disbelievers are burned in the Fire and their skins replaced so they continue tasting punishment, a direct instance of the source-section’s root ص ل ي and its enduring fire.
The verse contrasts the person cast into Fire with the one who comes safe on Judgment Day, closely matching the section’s wretch entering fire and the mindful person kept from it.

The disbelievers are brought to the Fire after enjoying worldly life and acting arrogantly; this makes a specific link between the section’s fire-bound person and the preference for nearer life described in 87:16.
Following God’s guidance means no going astray or being wretched; turning away leads into the hardship-and-fire sequence developed in 20:124–127 and the section’s ashqa contrast.
After God protects the givers from the Day’s evil in 76:11, this verse gives them gardens and silk, completing the protective reward linked to the section’s giver.
The human who is stingy when good reaches him sharpens the section’s contrast between the miser and the most mindful person spared from fire.
The righteous have a known share in their wealth, contrasting with the gatherer who hoards in 70:18 and the section’s fire-bound miser.
The wealth share is for the asker and deprived, specifying the giving that opposes the hoarding named just before the section’s fire scene.
The righteous affirm the Day of Judgment, the opposite of the section’s person who denies and turns away before the warning.
They fear their Lord’s punishment, giving the fear that motivates the section’s shield against the threatened fire.
The passage says no one is secure from the Lord’s punishment; this makes the section’s protective taqwa a needed response to the fire warning.
The people fail to urge feeding the poor, reversing the giving that marks the protected side of the section’s surah 92 contrast.
They consume inheritance greedily, extending the passage’s indictment of wealth-seeking before the Fire is brought near.
Their immense love of wealth specifies the worldly attachment behind the section’s gatherer who hoards before Leza calls.
Hell is brought near on that Day, completing the wealth indictment with the same approaching fire threatened in the section.
The person regrets not having sent deeds ahead for his life, sharpening the warning that worldly wealth cannot avail at the fall.
The condemned person is seized and bound, a concrete beginning to the punishment of the wretch who enters the section’s fire.
He is ordered into Hell, completing the seizure in 69:30 with the section’s central fire outcome.
The condemned did not believe in God, matching the section’s denied warning before the fire.
He did not urge feeding the poor, a specific reversal of the giving that marks the section’s protected side.
The sinner’s food in punishment is described as foul, continuing the fire-bound fate after the denial and withheld charity in 69:33–34.
Only sinners eat that punishment food, completing the section’s identification of the wretched person with the fire-bound end.
